title: Communicative Sciences & Disorders On-Campus MS Program Virtual Info Session
So You Want to Add a Generative-AI Component? Safety, Adversarial Testing, and the Preparation Phase
description: Hosted by the Center for Advancement and Dissemination of Intervention Optimization (CADIO)There is a growing interest in adding generative-AI components to existing behavioral or digital health interventions. However, conversational AI introduces failure modes, misinformation, missed escalation, and the cultivation of emotional dependency. This webinar makes the case that these risks are best surfaced during the preparation phase, before a system is ever optimized or placed in front of participants. Drawing on work developing a generative-AI assistant for a substance-use recovery platform, Drs. William Nardi and Annika Schoene will introduce a two-part approach to safety testing: first, attacking a system with validated single- and multi-turn adversarial prompts to confirm it clears established hurdles; and second, developing domain-specific "stress tests", grounded in clinical expertise and patient lived experience, that probe how a clinical condition can show up in conversation and challenge a system in subtler ways over time. A central theme is a distinction that reframes how we think about safety evidence, where a good adversarial test is defined by its validity, not by whether it breaks the system. Breaking a system in the lab is a useful and informative exercise, not a failure and helps to fix problems before real-world exposure. The talk closes by connecting these ideas back to optimization, where continuous safety monitoring can become one more criterion informing component-selection decisions.https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/16/so-you-want-add-generative-ai-component-safety-adversarial-testing (https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/16/so-you-want-add-generative-ai-component-safety-adversarial-testing)

title: Manual Cinema: The 4th Witch
description: ABOUT  Cameras roll, hands reach in, a shadow becomes a forest, a scrap of cardboard becomes a castle. You watch the movie get made. On a table full of overhead projectors, paper puppets, and tiny sets, the artists of Manual Cinema build Macbeth shot by shot in front of you, and a finished film assembles itself on the screen above. Immersive sound design and an original score are played live.  The story starts where Shakespeare's play ends. A girl loses her home and family to war, runs into the woods, and is taken in by three witches who feed her hunger for revenge on the warlord who did it. Shakespeare's tragedy unfolds somewhere offstage; The 4th Witch keeps its eye on the child left in the wreckage, and along the way, a taste for blood passes from one generation to the next. It is strange, handmade, and beautiful.ADVISORY  Recommended for ages 12 and up. There are loud sounds and flashing lights.RUN TIME  65 minutes

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

title: Translation Lecture Series: Translation and Justice in Socio-Environmental Conflicts
description: How can translators help co-create knowledge across communities and help broaden participation in climate justice processes? What goes into scientific and technical translation beyond knowledge of language and science? Is translation only a transfer of such knowledge or is it also a world-making practice? How can translators and researchers resist environmental injustice in and with communities that face the most impact? Drawing from her ethnographic research and her own practice, Piñeiro examines how translators and interpreters can use their research, language, and intercultural skills to be important allies in the work of environmental justice.  Sponsored by Critical Creative Production (https://liberalstudies.nyu.edu/academics/gls-curriculum/concentrations/critical-creative-production.html?challenge=d06e90d7-4d8f-4b88-9d8c-10b73beb60f1) and the Minor in Translation Studies (https://liberalstudies.nyu.edu/academics/minor-in-translation-studies.html?challenge=d06e90d7-4d8f-4b88-9d8c-10b73beb60f1), with support from the LS Programming and Events Committee. title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions. title: Polio Vaccines: Wanted Dead or Alive
description: Hosted by NYU Center for the HumanitiesA conversation featuring David Oshinsky, Frances Bernstein, Perri Klass, and Trace Jordan The development of polio vaccines in the 1950s gave the ability to protect children against a crippling and often fatal disease that had cast an ominous shadow for decades. But medical science had simultaneously generated two types of polio vaccine – one that contained killed polio virus, developed and championed by Dr. Jonas Salk, and one that included live but attenuated polio virus, discovered by his bitter rival and public critic, Dr. Albert Sabin. Prompted by a new biography of Sabin, this panel presentation explores the contrasting personalities of the two scientists, how the vaccines were originally tested (an unexpected excursion into the Soviet Union during the height of the Cold War), and the risks and benefits of each vaccine type. Debates and decisions about the optimal polio vaccine continue today, shaping the daily practice of pediatricians and public health workers throughout the United States and around the world. The event will feature NYU Professors David Oshinsky (Professor of History and Director of the Division of Medical Humanities at NYU Grossman School of Medicine), Frances Bernstein (Clinical Professor, Russian & Slavic Studies), and Perri Klass (Professor of Journalism and Pediatrics). The panel moderator is Trace Jordan (Clinical Professor, College Core Curriculum). Brought to you by the Medical Humanities Working Group.https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/20/polio-vaccines-wanted-dead-or-alive (https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/20/polio-vaccines-wanted-dead-or-alive)

title: ISAW Expanding the Ancient World Workshop: "From Silver Mines to the Palatine: Slavery in the Roman World"
description: Registration is required. Please fill out the form at the bottom of this page.   Expanding the Ancient World (https://isaw.nyu.edu/outreach) is a series of professional development workshops and online resources for teachers. Keyed to the NYC Department of Education Social Studies Scope and Sequence, this program is designed to offer K-12 educators opportunities to develop their knowledge of the ancient world and to provide classroom-ready strategies for teaching the past with reliable sources. Featuring inquiry-based workshops, flexible lesson plans, and up-to-date research, Expanding the Ancient World aims to equip teachers with information and skills that they can share with their students. CTLE credits will be offered to New York State teachers.  The workshop invites teachers to further incorporate Roman slavery into ancient history curricula. From transactional papyri, to clever slaves on stage, to the tombstone of a child miner, we will examine slavery both as a ubiquitous legal phenomenon and as a varied spectrum of experience across the Roman world. That is, we will engage with not just the testimonies of the literary elite—largely that of enslavers—but also traces of enslaved people's lives in material and visual culture. Grounded in a series of concrete case studies, we will discuss how to present primary sources that will require students to confront some of the most challenging, and fascinating, aspects of ancient history.  We will focus on several questions: What was slavery in the Roman Empire? Who was enslaved, and how did they become enslaved? How can we learn about them? What can studying Roman slavery contribute to our understanding of both slavery and Roman history? We will also analyze together how the ancient phenomenon differed from more recent slavery, such as the Transatlantic slave trade, because of the nature of different practices, evidence preservation, and conceptions of race and ethnicity. However, the legacy of ancient slavery had a profound impact on enslavers' worldviews in the Antebellum South and beyond; we will untangle historians' anachronistic assumptions to effectively, and critically, think across periods. Ultimately, the aim is to present students with an even deeper and more accurate understanding of everyday life and human experience in the ancient world.  Workshop led by Charlotte Mandy (https://classicalstudies.columbia.edu/students/charlotte-mandy) (PhD Student, Columbia University Classical Studies).  Participants will receive 1.5 CTLE hours.If you have any questions regarding the Expanding the Ancient World program please email ETAW@nyu.edu (mailto:ETAW@nyu.edu).Please check isaw.nyu.edu (http://isaw.nyu.edu/) for event updates.ISAW is committed to providing a positive and educational experience for all guests and participants who attend our public programming. We ask that all attendees follow the guidelines listed in our community standards policy (http://isaw.nyu.edu/events/community-standards-policy).

title: Where is the Care?
description: Dejha Carrington is an arts leader. In 2017, she co-founded Commissioner, a collaborative model and social practice that brings locals together to support contemporary artists and collect art in their cities. As Executive Director, she has cultivated a community of over 850 members to date, collectively funding more than 50 curated artist commissions in Miami, Detroit, Montréal, and Mexico City. From 2015 to 2022, she served as Vice President of Strategic Communications for YoungArts. She is CBVC's 2026–27 Distinguished Scholar-in-Residence and teaches the Business of Art at New World School of the Arts at Miami-Dade College, dividing her time between Miami, Montréal, and New York.Damien Davis is a Brooklyn-based artist and curator, born in Crowley, Louisiana and raised in Phoenix, Arizona. His practice explores historical representations of Blackness, unpacking the visual language of different cultures and questioning how those societies code and decode representations of race through craft, design, and digital modes of production. Using digital tools to shape layers of natural and synthetic materials, Davis composes stories through a lexicon of graphic figures and shapes that move between personal memory and chapters of human history, using color as both aesthetic and metaphor to create space for confronting bias and dehumanization in contemporary society.  His work has appeared at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Arts and Design, The Whitney Museum, and the Museum of Modern Art, as well as METHOD Gallery in Seattle and Biagiotti Progetto Arte in Italy. He holds a Master's degree in Visual Arts Administration from NYU and is the recipient of the Rema Hort Mann Foundation Community Engagement Grant, with residencies at the Museum of Arts and Design, Lower Manhattan Cultural Council, and Pilchuck Glass School. Davis is a former fellow and current advisor for the Art & Law Program in New York City. His work has been featured in The New York Times, Frieze Magazine, The Guardian, Hyperallergic, and Vulture.

This year, we are honored to have Christina Greer in conversation with Mitchell Moss, the Henry Hart Rice Professor of Urban Policy and Planning, to discuss public policy and urban politics.Christina Greer is a Professor of Political Science at Fordham University and an expert on urban politics and race. She is the author of Black Politics in Transition: Immigration, Suburbanization and Gentrification, and How to Build a Democracy: From Fannie Lou Hamer and Barbara Jordan to Stacey Abrams, and the co-editor of Black Ethnics: Race, Immigration and the Pursuit of the American Dream. Professor Greer is the inaugural Senior Policy Fellow at the Brooklyn Organization and the co-host of the podcast, FAQ: NYC.This event is for all NYU students, staff, faculty, and members of the broader community. The doors will open at 5:45pm.RSVP: https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/2026-henry-hart-rice-urban-policy-forum-2026-10-20 (https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/2026-henry-hart-rice-urban-policy-forum-2026-10-20)

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

title: Science, the Humanities, and Our Lives: Facing the Age of AI
description: Program:Opening Remarks by NYU Shanghai Provost Bei Wu (5 minutes)  Professor Ge Jianxiong's Keynote: "Science, the Humanities, and Our Lives: Navigating the Age of AI" (45 minutes)  A conversation between NYU Shanghai Chancellor Tong Shijun and Professor Ge Jianxiong (30 minutes)  Q&A (10 minutes)  Speaker Bio:  Professor Ge Jianxiong traces his ancestral roots to Shaoxing, Zhejiang Province. He holds a PhD in History and is the Library Director of The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; a Distinguished Senior Professor in the humanities and social sciences at Fudan University; a member of the History Division of the Ministry of Education's Social Sciences Committee; an advisory member of the National Social Science Fund's disciplinary office; and a Fellow of the Central Research Institute of Culture and History.  Professor Ge previously served as Director of Fudan University's Institute of Chinese Historical Geography and Director of its Research Center for Historical Geography, a Key Research Institute of the Ministry of Education. He has also served as Deputy Chair of the Ministry of Education's Committee on Academic Integrity; Chair of the Historical Geography Committee of the Geographical Society of China; Vice President of the Society for Qin and Han History Studies; a council member of the Chinese Historical Society; Vice President of the Shanghai Historical Society and the Shanghai Society for Social Science Popularization; and a counselor to the Shanghai Municipal Government. He was a member of the Standing Committee of the 12th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference.  From 2007 to 2014, he served as Library Director of Fudan University. During that period, he was also Deputy Chair of the Ministry of Education's Steering Committee for Academic Libraries and Vice President of the Shanghai Branch of the Library Society of China.

title: Is it time to merge?
description: Right now, many nonprofits are making hard choices about how to sustain their missions in the face of funding cuts and a changed funding environment. For some, that means considering whether a merger or collaborative venture could protect programs, preserve community relationships, and create a more durable path forward. In this panel, we'll talk candidly about what leads organizations to explore these options, what concerns or misconceptions can make the conversations difficult, and how leaders can approach the process with clarity, care, and a focus on what the community needs most.  In this session, we will explore:  - Why mergers and collaborative ventures matter now  - Common challenges and misconceptions  - What becomes possible when shared resources are aligned  - Tools for getting startedEvent series: Tough but important conversations shaping the future of the nonprofit sector  Nonprofit work is changing, and leaders need space to ask the questions that do not always have easy answers. This event series creates room for candid, thoughtful conversations about how nonprofits can adapt, collaborate, and build stronger paths toward mission impact. Together, we will explore the challenges, opportunities, and new ideas shaping the future of our work and what nonprofit leaders can do now to prepare for what comes next.This event series is offered in collaboration with theGeorge H. Heyman, Jr. Program for Philanthropy and Fundraisingwithin theNYU SPS Center for Global Affairs.

title: The Rise of Dominican American Political Power in the United States
description: In Politics in Our Veins, Yalidy Matos, Domingo Morel, and Michelle Bueno Vásquez chart the rise of Dominican American political power across the United States, exploring the myriad factors that have contributed to their political success as thoughtful citizens, activists, and elected officials. On October 21, join us for a panel conversation marking the publication of the new book with the authors alongside Ramona Hernandez, Raquel Batista, and Cristina Beltrán. This event takes place at NYU Wagner (105 East 17th Street). Doors will open at 5 pm, and the event begins at 5:30 pm.About the BookDominican Americans are one of the largest and fastest-growing Latinx groups in the United States, with a population that has quadrupled from 517,000 to a little over 2.3 million as of 2023. While New York City is home to the largest Dominican community in the country—and is where most Dominican American elected officials (DEOs) are from—Dominican Americans continue to increase their representation nationwide. Learn more via NYU Press.PanelistsRaquel Batista is an experienced civil rights and social impact leader in government, corporate and non-profit spaces. She previously served as the Commissioner of the NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs, as Executive Director of the Northern Manhattan Coalition for Immigrant Rights and more recently at the New York City Asylum Application Center assisting hundreds of recently arrived migrants with their humanitarian applications. A second-generation Afro-Dominicana, Latina, and lifelong New Yorker, Ms. Batista has been advocating for the rights of immigrant New Yorkers for over two decades.Ramona Hernández is a Distinguished Professor of Sociology and the Director of the CUNY Dominican Studies Institute, both at The City College of New York. She also holds faculty affiliations with the International Migration MA Program and the Sociology PhD Program at the CUNY Graduate Center. She is also the Executive Director of the Inter-University Program for Latino Research. Dr. Hernández's latest publication, From Immigrants to Settled People: Dominicans in the United States, co-authored with Gregory Morton, is forthcoming from Lived Places Publishing Press. She was also recently selected as one of the 2026 Latino Trailblazers by City & State New York.Yalidy Matos is Associate Professor of Political Science at Rutgers University. She is the author of Moral and Immoral Whiteness in Immigration Politics. Matos has been the recipient of the 2022 American Political Science Association Distinguished Junior Scholar in Political Psychology Award and a 2024-2025 Russel Sage Foundation Visiting Scholar.Domingo Morel is Associate Professor of Political Science and Public Service at the Robert F. Wagner School of Public Service at New York University. He is the author and co-editor of several books, including Takeover: Race, Education, and American Democracy, which won the W.E.B. Du Bois Distinguished Book Award, and most recently Developing Scholars: Race, Politics, and the Pursuit of Higher Education.Michelle Bueno Vásquez is a Doctoral Student in Political Science at Northwestern University.Cristina Beltrán works at the intersection of Latinx politics and political theory. She is an associate professor and director of graduate studies in the Department of Social and Cultural Analysis. Her work has appeared in Political Theory, the Du Bois Review, Aztlán: A Journal of Chicano Studies, Political Research Quarterly, and various edited volumes. She is currently the co-editor of Theory & Event, a peer-reviewed journal that publishes work by scholars working at the intersections of political theory, cultural theory, political economy, aesthetics, philosophy, and the arts. She is also an occasional guest on MSNBC.There will be a small reception to follow afterward.RSVP: https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/rise-dominican-american-political-power-united-states-2026-10-21 (https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/rise-dominican-american-political-power-united-states-2026-10-21)

title: ISAW Lecture: Burial and Betrayal Punishing Social Transgressions in the Ancient Roman Cemetery
description: Registration is required. Please fill out the form at the bottom of this page.Abstract  The ancient Roman cemetery is often framed as the domain of the "well deserving," as funerary monuments frequently formulaically assert. These dead were deserving of proper burial, of commemoration, and of the ongoing provision of offerings and other cult activities that both integrated them into the community of the dead and maintained their relationships with the living. But what might happen to the "badly deserving?" By examining select case studies of social betrayal documented in Roman cemeteries from the first three centuries CE, this talk will explore efforts at enforcing postmortem punishments against those perceived to have violated Roman social norms. It will argue that these stories of betrayal, while unique in their specifics, together illuminate the ways in which private individuals could seek to impose a form of afterlife exile upon those they deemed guilty of social transgressions.About the speaker  Darcy Tuttle is a Research Scholar at ISAW. Her research draws on historical, archaeological, epigraphic, and literary evidence to explore how people engaged with and related to the dead in the ancient Italy. She is an active field archaeologist with involvement in two projects based in Italy: the Gabii Project and the Southern Etruscan Tomb Survey. She recently completed her PhD at the University of California, Berkeley in the Graduate Group in Ancient History and Mediterranean Archaeology. Prior to joining ISAW, she was the recipient of the 2026 Donald and Maria Cox | Dorothy and Lewis B. Cullman Rome Prize at the American Academy in Rome. She is currently working on a book project provisionally entitled, "Ghost Justice: Crime, Community, and the Roman Cult of the Dead."Please check isaw.nyu.edu (http://isaw.nyu.edu/) for event updates.ISAW is committed to providing a positive and educational experience for all guests and participants who attend our public programming. We ask that all attendees follow the guidelines listed in our community standards policy (https://isaw.nyu.edu/events/community-standards-policy).

title: Saving St. Andrew's Chapel: Traversing the Heritage / Sustainability Pendulum in the UK Today
description: The presentation will explore the many, often conflicting heritage and sustainability challenges in bringing a derelict mediaeval chapel back into use as a contemporary home in rural England. British architect Malcolm Fryer will outline his work, focusing on the ongoing project to repair and improve the St. Andrew's Chapel at Boxley in Kent. He will share details about his work with Historic England on thermal, moisture and airtightness performance as a case study that suggests directions and practices for the integration of efficiency and modernization into historic structures. Professor Fryer will also share his experience in taking NYU MA students to visit the project over the last few years, highlighting opportunities to participate in projects, investigating and contributing to emerging practices in our field.  Sponsored by the NYU M.A. in Historical and Sustainable Architecture  If you do not hold a current NYU ID, please register here for building access:https://forms.gle/Ndwm2MTcf5dzzEzt9 (https://forms.gle/Ndwm2MTcf5dzzEzt9)

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

ENVIRONMENTAL CRISIS IN SOUTHEAST ASIA: POLITICS, MISRULE, AND RESISTANCE
description: This conference brings together scholars and practitioners to examine the politics of environmental crisis across Southeast Asia—a region where socio-ecological ruptures are not aberrations but products of longstanding structures of extraction and governance failure.Panelists trace the roots of these crises and assess how extractive industries, increasingly legitimized through the language of green transitions and climate finance, reproduce entrenched patterns of dispossession and injustice. From nickel mining and biofuel expansion to sand dredging and flood aid corruption, the panels situate contemporary crises within deeper histories of resource conflict and structural inequality.The conference foregrounds questions of resistance and accountability: what are communities, activists, and civil society organizations doing to contest new forms of ecological crisis? And what political conditions are necessary to advance climate action while achieving social and environmental justice? Beyond critical analysis, we seek insights into the strategies—legal, political, and grassroots—that have worked or might work to address Southeast Asia's intertwined ecological and democratic crises.RSVP: https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/environmental-crisis-southeast-asia-politics-misrule-and-resistance-2026-10-22 (https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/environmental-crisis-southeast-asia-politics-misrule-and-resistance-2026-10-22)

title: Hangeul Day
description: EAS Presents Hangeul DayDepartment of East Asian Studies (EAS), in collaboration with KISO, proudly presents Hangeul Day. Hangeul Day is a national holiday in South Korea, celebrated on October 9th each year. It commemorates the creation and proclamation of the Korean writing system, Hangeul, by King Sejong the Great in 1443. The day is marked by various cultural events, exhibitions, and educational programs that highlight the significance of Hangeul in Korean history and culture. The event will feature interactive Korean language workshop stations where participants can learn and practice the basics of Hangeul. Additionally, attendees can enjoy calligraphy, traditional crafts, games, and experience the elegance of hanbok, the traditional Korean attire. This celebration will be a vibrant showcase of Korean heritage and language. Come and join us! title: Power & Sample Size 1 & 2: The Basics & Simulation Methods
description: Hosted by the Department of BiostatisticsThis workshop is led by Chuck Huber, PhD, Director of Statistical Outreach, STATA CorpPower and Sample Size 1: The BasicsIn this talk I introduce the concepts and jargon of power and sample size calculations such as alpha levels, power, and minimum detectable effect sizes.  I do several simple calculations manually and then demonstrate how to replicate these calculations using Stata's -power- commands.  Next I demonstrate how to create tables and graphs for power, sample size, and minimum detectable effect sizes for a range of values.  We will conclude with a discussion of strategies to increase statistical power.Power and Sample Size 2: Simulation MethodsThis talk is a continuation of Power and Sample Size 1.  This talk demonstrates how to calculate power using simulation methods and how to create your own custom power calculation programs that leverage Stata's -power- command to create custom tables and graphs.  We will work examples that simulate power for a t-test, the interaction term in a linear regression model, and the interaction term in a multilevel model.  Along the way you will learn how to create simulated datasets, use Stata's -simulate- command, and how to write your own Stata commands using -program- and -syntax-.Chuck Huber, PhD is Director of Statistical Outreach at StataCorp and Adjunct Associate Professor of Biostatistics at the Texas A&M School of Public Health and at the New York University School of Global Public Health. He produces instructional videos for the Stata Youtube channel, writes blog entries, develops online NetCourses and gives talks about Stata at conferences and universities.  He has published in the areas of neurology, human and animal genetics, alcohol and drug abuse prevention, nutrition and birth defects.This workshop is open to NYU GPH students and faculty only.https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/22/power-sample-size-1-2-basics-simulation-methods (https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/22/power-sample-size-1-2-basics-simulation-methods)

title: Navigating Global Challenges—Rethinking Readiness with Jeff Schlegelmilch
description: As the nature of disasters becomes increasingly complex—from climate-driven hazards and pandemics to cascading infrastructure failures, geopolitical instability, and systemic disruption—traditional approaches to preparedness are being challenged. Mr. Schegelmilch will offer a forward-looking perspective on what it means to be truly ready in an era of interconnected and compounding risks.  This thought-provoking conversation will explore how governments, businesses,  communities, and individuals can rethink readiness—not simply as the ability to respond to a known hazard, but as the capacity to anticipate uncertainty, adapt to disruption, and build resilience before crisis strikes.  In this session, Chloe Demrovsky, Executive in Residence and Clinical Visiting  Assistant Professor in Global Business and Economy at NYU SPS Center for Global Affairs, will engage Mr. Schegelmilch in a dynamic conversation drawing on his extensive experience in disaster preparedness, resilience, emergency management, and risk reduction. Together, they will examine what the next generation of readiness should look like—and how we can move from preparing for individual disasters to building systems capable of navigating a world of cascading and interconnected risks.  This roundtable is part of a series of intimate discussions with influential figures shaping the future of the global economy.

title: An Evening with Anne Fadiman: Looking back on The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down after three decades
description: Nearly thirty years ago, Fadiman's sensitive story of Lia Lee, a Hmong child with epilepsy, and her American doctors, brought the complexities of cross-cultural medicine to a wide audience and changed the way that medicine is practiced and understood in the United States.  The book continues to be taught at universities both as literary journalism and as a casebook for cross-cultural practice in general; it is also widely read by medical students and practitioners who wish to offer more effective care to patients from other cultures.  As The New York Times' obituary of Lia Lee noted, "Lia's story, as few other narratives have done, has had a significant effect on the ways in which American medicine is practiced across cultures, and on the training of doctors."  On October 22, Fadiman will speak with NYU Professor Perri Klass about how the book came to be, and how its lessons about medicine, culture, and care still resonate today.   REGISTER HERE (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/2001217809339?aff=oddtdtcreator)

title: Rabih Mroué & Lina Majdalanie: Four Walls and a Roof
description: ABOUT  In 1947, Bertolt Brecht sat before the House Un-American Activities Committee and ran rings around it: playing dumb, parsing translations, denying he had written what he had written, until the chairman thanked him for his cooperation. Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie take that hearing, already a theatrical encounter, and turn it into a piece of theater. What they build from it is funny in a bleak way and pointed in a serious one: a look at how an artist talks his way out of a room, and what it costs him.  Mroué and Majdalanie are Lebanese artists who spent years making theater in Beirut before the pressures of working there drove them to Berlin, and they set that departure alongside Brecht's. His evening in Washington starts to mirror their own exile: two generations of artists weighing what they can say against what it will cost them. What does a person tell the state when it demands an answer, and what do they surrender to keep speaking?LANGUAGE  Performed in English, with German songs with English surtitlesRUN TIME  1 hour and 40 minute

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL CRISIS IN SOUTHEAST ASIA: POLITICS, MISRULE, AND RESISTANCE
description: This conference brings together scholars and practitioners to examine the politics of environmental crisis across Southeast Asia—a region where socio-ecological ruptures are not aberrations but products of longstanding structures of extraction and governance failure.Panelists trace the roots of these crises and assess how extractive industries, increasingly legitimized through the language of green transitions and climate finance, reproduce entrenched patterns of dispossession and injustice. From nickel mining and biofuel expansion to sand dredging and flood aid corruption, the panels situate contemporary crises within deeper histories of resource conflict and structural inequality.The conference foregrounds questions of resistance and accountability: what are communities, activists, and civil society organizations doing to contest new forms of ecological crisis? And what political conditions are necessary to advance climate action while achieving social and environmental justice? Beyond critical analysis, we seek insights into the strategies—legal, political, and grassroots—that have worked or might work to address Southeast Asia's intertwined ecological and democratic crises.RSVP: https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/environmental-crisis-southeast-asia-politics-misrule-and-resistance-2026-10-23 (https://wagner.nyu.edu/community/events/environmental-crisis-southeast-asia-politics-misrule-and-resistance-2026-10-23)

title: Bioethics Colloquium: On Chaos, What we Ought to Do, and What we Ought to Regret
description: Hosted by the Center for BioethicsJoin the NYU Center for Bioethics for a colloquium with Caspar Hare, Professor of Philosophy in the Department of Linguistics and Philosophy at MIT, whose work spans ethics, practical rationality, and metaphysics. Drawing on his new book, Living in a Strange World, Professor Hare will explore a striking idea: for almost every action ever taken, future generations can correctly say that if it had not happened, they almost certainly would not exist. He argues that this has no surprising implications for what we ought to do, but very surprising implications for what we ought to regret. Attendees will see how big ideas from cosmology, physics, and metaphysics can bear on everyday moral life, and how they might change the way we think about past wrongs and our own existence. The talk will be followed by a reception.https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/23/bioethics-colloquium-chaos-what-we-ought-do-and-what-we-ought-regret (https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/23/bioethics-colloquium-chaos-what-we-ought-do-and-what-we-ought-regret)

title: Rabih Mroué & Lina Majdalanie: Four Walls and a Roof
description: ABOUT  In 1947, Bertolt Brecht sat before the House Un-American Activities Committee and ran rings around it: playing dumb, parsing translations, denying he had written what he had written, until the chairman thanked him for his cooperation. Rabih Mroué and Lina Majdalanie take that hearing, already a theatrical encounter, and turn it into a piece of theater. What they build from it is funny in a bleak way and pointed in a serious one: a look at how an artist talks his way out of a room, and what it costs him.  Mroué and Majdalanie are Lebanese artists who spent years making theater in Beirut before the pressures of working there drove them to Berlin, and they set that departure alongside Brecht's. His evening in Washington starts to mirror their own exile: two generations of artists weighing what they can say against what it will cost them. What does a person tell the state when it demands an answer, and what do they surrender to keep speaking?LANGUAGE  Performed in English, with German songs with English surtitlesRUN TIME  1 hour and 40 minute

title: Vitalisms II
description: Vitalisms II is an exhibition-as-experiment that continues a long-term research and education project on contemporary painting in China. Following the first chapter's inquiry into the historicity of painting, we now turn toward a different question: How does valuecome into being through our encounters with painting?  As the opening season of our new artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), Vitalisms II considers inheritance as a condition we inhabit and reinterpret. Within the financial imagination, value is rendered calculable, comparable, and exchangeable. Yet value can also name artistic, historical, social, institutional, and affective relations. What happens when a painting is encountered as an artwork, cultural artifact, collectible object, commodity, or financial asset?Vitalisms II focuses on abstract and non-representational painting, a field whose boundaries remain uncertain. The exhibition brings together practices ranging from conceptually driven, hard-edged geometric painting to more intuitive and expressive approaches, including works that approach the threshold of representation. How might abstraction reveal, rather than obscure, relations that are otherwise difficult to perceive? How might we keep interpretation open, rather than seeking settlement? And what might speculation come to mean as a practice of imagining otherwise, rather than predicting return?  The title Vitalisms draws from Isabelle Graw's account of painting's "vitalistic fantasies"—how vitality and agency have been projected onto painting. *Vitalisms I asked whether we could extend these fantasies and think of paintings as active participants in the historical and social relations through which they are made, encountered, and circulated. Vitalisms II asks: What might happen when we approach a painting not simply as an image to be interpreted, but as something with which we enter into relation?  Like the first Vitalisms, this chapter is conceived as an experiment in which knowledge is exchanged and produced throughout the exhibition. During weekly study sessions, we spend extended time with the paintings, developing interpretations collectively through close looking, discussion, and reflection. These encounters become part of the exhibition's research, inviting us to ask: What might we come to value—and, in turn, make possible?  * Isabelle Graw, The Love of Painting (Sternberg Press, 2018): 21-24.——————————————————���——————————————————–Vitalisms II is accompanied by related events, including:  OPENING RECEPTIONFriday, 18 September, 16:00–19:00        A public reception to celebrate the exhibition's opening with food and drinks.STUDY SESSION (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/form-and-content-ii)  Form & Content II: How Do We Value Painting(s)?Fridays, 13:00–14:00 (English) / 16:00–17:00 PM (Chinese)      9, 16, 23, 30 October      6, 13, 20 November        For the artwork featured in each session and the full schedule, please visit the event webpage.  A weekly series of Study Sessions facilitated by ICA curators using Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS). Each one-hour session focuses on a single painting, inviting participants to spend time looking and sharing their observations and interpretations through conversation. The sessions bring the public into Vitalisms II's research into how value comes into being through our encounters with painting. No prior knowledge of art or the exhibition is required.ROUNDTABLE (https://ica.shanghai.nyu.edu/program/after-looking)  After Looking: What Does Looking Have to Do with Value?Saturday, 5 December, 13:30-17:00        A roundtable bringing together the artists exhibiting in Vitalisms II and the ICA curators who facilitated the exhibition's Study Sessions. Over seven weeks, the public spent sustained time with individual paintings through close looking and group discussion. From these sessions, the curators will bring selected observations, interpretations, and questions into conversation with the artists, exploring how paintings acquire meaning and value through different encounters.  All events are FREE and OPEN to the public.  For further details and to register for events, please visit the event pages under Related programs below.  —————————���———————————————————————��———–  The exhibition Vitalisms II and related events are presented as the first season of the ICA's artistic research program Untimely Inheritances (2026–28), attending to what inheritance asks of us and how we might inhabit unfinished worlds through practices of interpretation, response, and transformation.Vitalisms II is organized by Michelle Yeonho Hyun with BAO Yang and CHEN Baichao, with additional support by HOU Chuchu, QU Yanqiu and JIAO Meiqi. Special thanks to Arts & Collections Foundation, Luoying Sheng, Han Xiao, and Chong Zhou for their generosity, as well as Antenna Space, CLC Gallery, Magician Space, Ota Fine Arts, ShanghART Gallery and ZIAN Gallery, for their support. Graphic Design by LIU Anqi. Exhibition Design by FANG Yuan.  Our deepest gratitude belongs to the artists for sharing their knowledge, work, and time with us, extending our curiosity and creating more questions.  Early research and development for Untimely Inheritances received kind support from Goethe-Institut, as well as research assistance from Oviya Dinakhar, Fay Guan, and Lizzy Xie.

title: NYU Alumni and Families Weekend: Generally Recognized as "Safe"? Debunking the Myths of U.S. Food Regulation
description: Join us for NYU's Alumni & Families Weekend 2026 to reconnect with fellow GPH alumni! For decades, a regulatory loophole has allowed the food industry to introduce hundreds of new chemical substances directly into our food supply without ever notifying the public or the FDA. How did we get here, and what does it mean for the future of public health? NYU School of Global Public Health Professor Jennifer Pomeranz will take you behind the headlines to reveal how the "Generally Recognized As Safe" loophole works, why it primarily impacts ultra-processed foods, and the policy reforms required to fix a broken system.https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/24/nyu-alumni-and-families-weekend-generally-recognized-safe-debunking (https://publichealth.nyu.edu/events-news/events/2026/10/24/nyu-alumni-and-families-weekend-generally-recognized-safe-debunking)

title: Discover NY: Fall for Governors Island!
description: This event is intended for NYU international students/scholars and the NYU community.  Trade the subway for a ferry. Just 7 minutes from Lower Manhattan, Governors Island has 172 car-free acres and the best Statue of Liberty views in the city, and we're heading there on its most festive weekend of the fall.  For one weekend only, Nolan Park, just a 3-minute walk from the ferry, becomes a free pumpkin patch and fall festival (event page (https://www.govisland.com/things-to-do/events/pumpkin-point-2026)). Pick your own pumpkin and paint it, go trick-or-treating at the historic houses, and catch a ghost tour, a fall foliage walk or some live folk music.

title: 2026 Jesse Owens Track & Field Youth Program - Fall
description:
Join the Randall’s Island Park Alliance and City Parks Foundation for the Jesse Owens Track and Field Youth Program! This free weekly program is available to youth ages 8-16 and enables participants to learn the fundamentals of the sport and stay active. Activities will focus on running techniques for sprints and relays and will introduce other track and field activities like long jump, hurdles, and long-distance running.  
Program Dates:  Every Saturday 
Spring: 4/11 – 6/20, no program on 5/23  
Fall:  9/12 – 10/31  
Registration is required on LeagueApps with City Parks Foundation.  
Location: Thomas Jefferson Park 
For inquiries about accessibility, to request an accommodation or for event information, please email publicprograms@randallsisland.org.

title: Team RIVER Volunteers
description:
Volunteer with Team RIVER (Randall’s Island Volunteer Ecological Restorers) and help keep Randall’s Island Park beautiful! Team RIVER Volunteers regularly work with the Natural Areas team twice a month to take care of and restore our natural spaces on the island. With our Horticulture team, volunteers care for the many gardens, green streets and meadows, every second Wednesday of each month. Team RIVER also works with our Sports Field and Operations teams, keeping our park clean and maintained. If you are only able to volunteer on a limited basis, you are still very much welcome! 
This volunteer opportunity is open to individuals from the community. Groups of more than 5 people must contact: Volunteers@RandallsIsland.org 
Volunteers must be at least 11 years old. Anyone under the age of 18 must have a waiver signed by their legal guardian before starting any work. Children under 16 must also have an adult with them while volunteering. A downloadable volunteer waiver can be found at this link: General Volunteer – Randall’s Island 
Registration is required here. 
Location: Volunteers will be notified after registration. 
For inquiries about accessibility, to request an accommodation, or for event information, please email publicprograms@randallsisland.org.

title: DroneArt Show: Harry Potter™
description:
Watch 1,200 illuminated drones light up the night sky in a 60-minute open-air show set to the iconic music of the Harry Potter™ films, with a live electric violinist on stage! 
The drones take flight in perfect synchronization to recreate some of the most beloved moments from the wizarding world in breathtaking formations of light. Settle in on the lawn or in the seating area — pure wonder, nostalgia and enchantment, on a scale you won’t forget. 
Enjoy treats and other delights. The perfect way to start the night before the show. Butterbeer™ will be available at select venues. 
Take home a souvenir celebrating the world of Harry Potter™ with exclusive merchandise: wands, scarves and collectibles designed for fans of all ages. 
Learn more and buy tickets here: https://feverup.com/m/746195 
Location: Randall’s Island Park, Sunken Meadow Fields

title: 2026 Jesse Owens Track & Field Youth Program at Boo Bash!
description:
Join the Randall’s Island Park Alliance and City Parks Foundation for the Jesse Owens Track and Field Youth Program! This free weekly program is available to youth ages 8-16 and enables participants to learn the fundamentals of the sport and stay active. Activities will focus on running techniques for sprints and relays and will introduce other track and field activities like long jump, hurdles, and long-distance running.  
This week’s event will take place before our annual Boo Bash event at Randall’s Island Park! 
Registration is required on LeagueApps with City Parks Foundation.  
Location: Hilltop Picnic Area/Urban Farm 
For inquiries about accessibility, to request an accommodation or for event information, please email publicprograms@randallsisland.org.

description:
